content: Euphorbia peplus, commonly known as Petty Spurge, is a plant species belonging to the genus Euphorbia. It is native to a wide range of regions, including most of Europe, northern Africa, and western Asia. This plant typically thrives in cultivated arable land, gardens, and other disturbed areas. It is important to note that Euphorbia peplus should not be confused with Euphorbia peplis, also known as Purple Spurge, despite the similarity in their names. Euphorbia peplus is an annual plant that grows to a height of approximately 5 to 30 centimeters. Plants that grow as weeds in cultivated areas tend to be on the smaller end of this range. The stems of the plant are smooth and lack any hair. Its leaves are oval in shape with pointed tips (oval-acute), measuring 1 to 3 centimeters in length, and have smooth margins. The plant produces green flowers arranged in three-rayed umbels. The glands, which are characteristic of the Euphorbiaceae family, are kidney-shaped and feature long, thin horns. The plant exudes a milky latex sap, which is toxic. This sap has been traditionally used as a therapeutic agent for the removal of warts on the skin. Recent research also indicates that it may have efficacy in the treatment of superficial basal cell carcinomas. Outside its native range, Euphorbia peplus has become widely naturalized and is often considered invasive. It has established itself in various regions, including Australia, New Zealand, North America, and other countries with temperate and subtropical climates.
